title: TA8-10977
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the principal claimant), XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of Colombia, and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Mexico, claim to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

The claim of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of the U.S.A., was disjoined and rendered a negative bench decision on the basis of his U.S. citizenship. He is the son of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his designated representative. He is a minor.

The principal claimant is a 54-year-old formerly unemployed salesman from XXXXX, Colombia. He is accompanied by his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his daughter, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his daughter's son, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his daughter's Mexican husband, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and his daughter's U.S.-born son, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. He said that, in XXXXX 1999, he started receiving telephone calls from the United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia - AUC, paramilitaries) demanding that he stop his community work with the Patriotic Union (Movimiento Político Unión Patriótica, MPUP) in the town of XXXXX, threatening him if he did not comply. He said that he stopped his community work after that first call, but he received three others. He moved his family from XXXXX to XXXXX, then to XXXXX.

On XXXXX, 1999, he and his family left the country for the U.S.A. He said that his wife's brother-in-law, XXXXX XXXXX, had received a death letter from the AUC in XXXXX 2000 declaring the principal claimant a military objective (death sentence). His daughter met and married her Mexican husband, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, in the U.S.A. XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX bases his claim on the principal claimant's story.

The panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection for the reason that the panel does not find certain key aspects of the principal claimant's story credible or their fear well founded. Alternatively, the panel finds there is a viable internal flight alternative for them in Colombia. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimants' identities as citizens of their respective countries have been established by certified copies of their country passports and other identification documents tendered into evidence.2 Nexus

The panel finds this case has no connection to any of the Convention grounds based on the credibility findings below. In any case, the panel considers the analyses on credibility-well foundedness of fear and subjective fear to be applicable on either section 96 or 97(1). Credibility / Well-foundedness of the Claimants' Fear

The determinative issue in this case is credibility as to the well-foundedness of the claimants' fear. The panel finds the principal claimant's story not to be wholly credible as to the well-foundedness of their fear due to the following reasons.

When the panel asked the principal claimant if he complied with the AUC's demand to discontinue his voluntary community work, he replied that, "From XXXXX after the first call, I did not go back ever to visit any community." He had said that the first call from the AUC was on XXXXX, 1999, at his place of employment. When asked if he had therefore complied with the AUC's demand, he replied, "That's correct." When asked further if he believed that the AUC would know that he had complied with their demand, he said, "Yes, I do believe, Mr. Chair." Since this was the case, that he had complied with their demand, the panel finds it hard to believe that the AUC would continue to call him with threatening calls regarding his community work or even write him a sufragio (death note).3 Furthermore, in light of this serious doubt, the panel notes that the sufragio or death note appears to have been typed on a computer or electric typewriter, without anything on its appearance, which would persuade the panel to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that it was authentic. The panel, therefore, does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant and, by extension, his co-claimants, are targets of the AUC.

Furthermore, when asked if the AUC had ever confronted him personally, he said, "no." The panel finds it incredible that the AUC would, as he alleges, keep on calling and threatening him from XXXXX 1999 up to the time he left Colombia on XXXXX, 1999 without confronting him or a member of his family personally, wasting their time and effort on phone calls for no apparent purpose, as he had already complied with their demand to stop his community involvement shortly after XXXXX 1999. Furthermore, as he alleges, the AUC, through their network of infiltrators, would have been able to confirm his having stopped his community activities at the time. Furthermore, neither his parents in XXXXX nor his wife's brother-in-law, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, who filed a denunciation with the police against the AUC threats on his behalf after they had left Colombia, had been personally confronted by the AUC looking for him and his family or in retaliation for having filed a denunciation against the AUC. Based on these, the panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are targets of the AUC.

Furthermore, he had said that at the beginning of 2000, he sought the advice of a lawyer in the U.S., who encouraged him to gather as much evidence in support of filing an asylum claim in the U.S. In this regard, he had requested his wife's brother-in-law, Mr. Quiceno, to file a denunciation4 with the police on his behalf, which Mr. XXXXX did. He admitted that the police accepted the report but took no action on the complaint. The panel views this report with scepticism, as it appears to be a document of convenience. It is possible that Mr. XXXXX managed to request an official at the police station to prepare the document, which did not bear any official police letterhead and/or a rubber stamp showing it as having been received. However, the panel notes the complaint was only filed because the principal claimant needed it to add to his documentation for his U.S. claim. The panel, therefore, believes that, on a balance of probabilities, the denunciation did not reflect a real threat to the principal claimant but was simply a document produced for the purpose of providing support to his asylum claim.

He had indicated that he had heard about other members of the Patriotic Union, who had been killed over the years and that he knew these were done by the AUC, although the police had never positively identified the AUC as being the killers. When asked why he was so sure it was the AUC and not the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC, guerrillas), who were also known to go against community workers or volunteers,5 he said that he knew it was the AUC. However, the panel believes he appeared to be guessing or generalizing and that, on a balance of probabilities, the principal claimant was attempting to embellish his claim by making it appear that the AUC had targeted all Patriotic Union members, and he was, therefore, at risk.

From the totality of the foregoing evidence adduced, the panel does not find the claimant to be fully credible as to the objective basis of his claim and, further, believes, on a balance of probabilities, his fear not to be well founded. Subjective Fear - Not Claiming in the U.S.A.

When they arrived in the U.S.A., the principal claimant said that he did not file an asylum claim, as he said that he had heard that many Colombians had been deported by U.S. immigration officials. When he finally did consult a lawyer and managed to gather some documents in support of his claim, he said that the lawyer told him he was too late, since the deadline of one year for him to file an asylum claim had passed. However, the panel finds this lack of effort to find out and file his claim in time troubling and not demonstrative of the existence of his fear. It is a reasonable expectation that a person with genuine fear of persecution or harm in his home country will, absent a good reason, seek refugee protection immediately upon arrival in a safe country.6 The fact that he did not take this step soon upon arrival in the U.S.A. puts into question the genuineness of his fear. From the panel's view, the apparent lack of urgency in his actions belies his claim of fear.

Professor Hathaway has said that it is appropriate to inquire into the circumstances of any protracted postponement of a refugee claim as a means of evaluating the sincerity of the claimant's need for protection.7

In Leon, the claimant waited over five years to make a claim. In this case, the claimants lived in the U.S.A. over nine years without making a claim. Justice Muldoon of the Federal Court commented: It is incredible that he [the claimant] would believe that he could not make a refugee claim because he was an illegal.... That is incredible. That he would wait for five years in that belief, if that belief were true, is even more incredible.8

In Gonzalez, the claimant, who based her claim on a fear of a paramilitary group lived four years and three months in the U.S.A. without making a claim. The judgement indicated that "a delay over 4 years suggests a lack of subjective fear and it was open to the Board to reject the applicant's explanations."9
In the case at hand, the claimants exhibited a serious lack of urgency and inaction on making a claim in the U.S.A.
The panel, therefore, finds that there is neither a credible objective basis to their fear nor does it believe the existence of their subjective fear. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) - Bogota

If the foregoing were not at issue, IFA is. The panel finds that the claimants can settle today in Bogota, the country's capital, even if the principal claimant's assertion that the AUC is after him and his family was true, which the panel does not believe to be the case. The panel finds that he can relocate to Bogota, a megapolis of over 8 million people, about four times that of Toronto.

He said that he believes the AUC can trace him anywhere in the country, more so in the city of Bogota. However, the panel notes that he did not give any details or evidence on how the AUC would be able to do that other than saying that they were able to phone him when he moved to XXXXX, which the panel does not believe to be the case, and the panel believes, on a balance of probabilities, that he was and had been embellishing his claim. A common assertion is the fact that the AUC may have sophisticated databases for tracking targets down.

However, taking into account the fact that the entire country has 45 million people and Bogota alone has a mass of 8 million people, and the AUC had largely demobilized since laying down their arms in 2006, the panel finds it hard to believe that the AUC people who he said had targeted him, even if it were true, which the panel does not believe to be the case, would still have the capability to track him down if he and his family were to settle in Bogota today.

In considering if the claimants can find adequate protection from the state while living in Bogota, the panel has taken into account the following points. * Colombia is a constitutional democracy. * The most recent elections were considered to be generally fair and free and took place in an atmosphere of freedom, transparency and normalcy.10 * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of multi-level security forces consisting of local, national police forces and a national army.11 * The national police are responsible for internal law enforcement, shared with the Department of Administrative Security and the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators.12 * A new criminal procedure code has been in place since January 2008, resulting in shorter pretrial waiting periods and a conviction rate of 60% as opposed to the previous rate of 3%.13

The Prosecutor General's Office runs a witness protection program.14 The Prosecutor General's Office investigates criminal offences. Its Human Rights Unit, located in 13 satellite offices throughout the country, specializes in investigating human rights crimes. As of December 2008, 101 specialized prosecutors were handling 4,500 cases.15

There were incidents in the past and in 2008 when elements of the security forces acted in violation of state policy, the law and/or accepted rules of engagement. Many procedures are now in place to provide recourse to the rule of law for victims, for example: * The Ministry of Defense investigated personnel suspected of collaboration with new right-wing paramilitary groups, and culpable parties were handed over to civilian authorities. * Military or civilian authorities investigated killings committed by security forces. * Military and police accused of torture were now tried in civilian rather than military courts. * During 2008, the Ministry of Defense relieved from duty 80 officers and 213 NCO and soldiers for unethical conduct.16
These efforts have resulted in fewer killings by security forces in 2008 than in 2007.17

This review of the United States, Department of State, Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 200818 strongly indicates that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to security forces when they require protection from criminal acts and human rights investigators for protection from human rights abuse. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law.

Historically, Colombians have feared the left-wing guerrillas, the FARC, the National Liberation Army (ELN) and right-wing paramilitary groups such as the AUC. Many governments in the past took steps to control the FARC, the ELN and the AUC with marginal success. Since 2002, however, the current government, with the assistance of the U.S.A., has committed significant resources to protecting its citizens from harm from the militant groups. Even if there are reports today that renegade bands of the AUC had not participated in the demobilization, the fact that they had splintered away from the demobilized mainstream AUC, who were known to have collaborated with government forces against the left-wing FARC and ELN, and focused more on extortions and drug-trafficking to enrich themselves, leads the panel to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that these remnants are no more than common criminals rather than ideologically-based groups. 19

The panel cites the following points with respect to the current National Documentation Package on Colombia20 as follows: * While the previous 2005 UNHCR report of March 2005, in paragraph 58, said that, "The irregular armed groups have the capacity to track down victims throughout Colombia and indeed have done so frequently in the past," such reference no longer exists in the current report published four years later by the same agency. The panel is satisfied that this reference has been removed since it no longer applies. * Of particular interest in the current Exhibit R/A-1 are two reports by the International Crisis Group 4.1 from April 2008 and 4.5 from March 2009. Both are recent and all statements fully documented. Furthermore, the Group is guided by well-known and respected international personalities, including a former Prime Minister of Canada and an internationally recognized Canadian jurist.

Therefore, as far as Bogota is concerned, the panel finds that the area would be a reasonable one for the claimant considering that it has a large population of over 8 million and has reasonable security and social services capable of meeting the needs of its inhabitants. Having lived and, in all practicality, survived in the U.S.A. for over nine years, the panel believes, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants would be able to settle relatively well in Bogota. The panel also finds that Bogota would meet both requirements of a viable IFA for them.

Consequently, based on the totality of the evidence adduced, including Counsel's submission, the panel is not persuaded to believe that the claimants face persecution on a Convention ground or a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, should they be returned to Colombia.

As far as XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, the principal claimant's son-in-law, is concerned, when Counsel for the claimants asked him if he had any fear of persecution if he were returned to Mexico, he said, "no, no fear of persecution of any kind." He said that after about 2-3 years re-establishing his residency in Mexico, he would be able to petition his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and their child, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, who is a citizen of the U.S.A. for residency in Mexico.

On the basis of his testimony, the panel finds that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX faces no serious harm or persecution if he returned to Mexico and believes, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be able to petition for residency in Mexico his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and their child, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, who is also a U.S. citizen.

The Refugee Protection Division determines that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX are neither Convention refugees within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor persons in need of protection under subsection 97(1).
